A dribble is a small, thin, slow trickle of liquid. It is not a flow, not a stream, not a splash — it is the tiniest, most sluggish version of liquid moving. Think of it as the opposite of a flood. If a flood is a river bursting its banks, a dribble is a single bead of water slowly crawling down a surface.

The word always carries the sense of smallness and slowness. Keep that in mind — it runs through every meaning.
Meaning 1 — A thin trickle of liquid

A dribble is a tiny, slow amount of liquid falling or running from something.

"There was a dribble of olive oil down the side of the bottle."
"A dribble of water leaked from the old tap."
"He noticed a dribble of gravy on the tablecloth."

Imagine pouring sauce on your food and a tiny bit escapes and runs down the bottle, or the side of your plate. That thin, slow trail is a dribble. It is not enough to be a real spill. It is small, a little messy, and slightly uncontrolled.
Meaning 2 — Saliva or drool escaping from the mouth

This is the most frequently used meaning in everyday life. A dribble is saliva that leaks out of someone's mouth unintentionally, in a thin trickle.

"The baby had a dribble on its chin."
"She wiped away the dribble before he noticed."
"The dog left a dribble on the floor while staring at the food."

This happens with babies (who cannot yet control their mouth muscles), with sleeping people, with animals excited by food, or sometimes with elderly people or people who are unwell. It is not a dramatic pour of saliva — it is a thin, slow, involuntary trickle.

In British English especially, this is an extremely common use of the word. British people might say "wipe that dribble off your chin" without any hesitation.
Meaning 3 — A very small amount of something (used figuratively)

Because a dribble of liquid means a very small, slow trickle, English speakers also use the word to describe a very small, frustratingly slow amount of anything — not just liquid.

"Only a dribble of information was released to the public."
"She received a dribble of replies to her job applications."
"The government promised help, but delivered only a dribble of funds."

Here, the word is doing something clever. It is borrowing the physical image of a tiny, slow liquid trickle and applying it to abstract things like news, money, support, or progress. When something comes in a dribble, it is arriving too slowly and in too small a quantity to be satisfying. There is an undertone of frustration or disappointment in this usage.
Meaning 4 — A sports move (football and basketball)

In sports, a dribble is the noun form of the act of moving a ball forward through skill and control, without passing or kicking it hard.

In football (soccer): A dribble is when a player moves forward while keeping close control of the ball, tapping it with their feet past one or more opponents.

"His dribble past the last defender was extraordinary."
"That was the best dribble I have ever seen."

In basketball: A dribble is a single instance of bouncing the ball on the floor. The player keeps control of the ball by repeatedly bouncing it while moving.

"He lost the ball on his very first dribble."
"Her dribble is one of the best in the league."

In both sports, a dribble is about controlled, skillful movement — the player keeps the ball close and moves it forward without giving it to someone else or losing it.

Every meaning of dribble as a noun shares a common thread: something small, slow, and in a thin trickle. Whether it is liquid, saliva, information, or a sports move — a dribble is never large, never fast, and never a rush. It is always measured and slight.

When you see this word, ask yourself: what is the thin, slow, small trickle here? That will always point you to the right meaning.

• A baby or dog → drool/saliva coming from the mouth
  • A bottle of sauce or a leaking tap → a thin trail of liquid
  • News, money, or progress arriving slowly → a very small, unsatisfying amount
  • Football or basketball → a skilled, controlled move with the ball
